transcript.content: Hello
Hello Elizabeth! It's good to see you again. How have things been going since we last spoke? Is there anything particular on your mind today that you'd like to talk about?

Hey. Things have been… quiet, I guess. Like the kind of quiet that feels heavy instead of peaceful. I’ve been thinking a lot about how I talk to people lately. Not just what I say, but how I say it.  

Last week, I told my partner about a little thing that bothered me at work, and I went on a bit about it—like, why it mattered, how it made me feel, all of it. And he just said, “It’s not a big deal,” kind of casually. And I felt… like I’d overreacted. Like I’d made too much of it.  

Now I’m second-guessing everything. Am I too much? Too sensitive? Or do I just need to stop trying so hard to explain myself?  

I don’t want to shut down, but I also don’t want to feel like I’m being dismissed just because I’m honest.

Thank you for sharing that, Elizabeth. That "heavy quiet" you described — I can feel how much you've been sitting with this. It sounds like this one moment with your partner has really sent you spiraling into some deeper questions about yourself and how you show up with people.

I want to slow down for a second, because I noticed something important. You told your partner about something that bothered you, and you explained *why* it mattered and *how it made you feel*. That's actually... really healthy communication. You weren't just venting — you were trying to help him understand your experience.

And when he said "It's not a big deal," the message you received wasn't just about that one work situation, was it? It felt like he was saying something about *you* — that your feelings were too big, too much.

Can I ask — in that moment, when he said that, what did you do? Did you keep talking, did you go quiet, did something shift in you?

I just… stopped. Like my words got stuck in my throat. I didn’t say anything else. Just nodded. Smiled, even.  

And then I started talking about something else — the grocery list, or the weather — just to fill the silence.  

It wasn’t a big deal, right? I mean, it really wasn’t. But it felt like the air went out of the room. Like I’d said something too much, and now I had to fix it by pretending it didn’t matter.  

I don’t know why I do that. I want to be real, but then I panic if it doesn’t land the way I hope. So I shrink. I make it small. I make it easy for them to brush off.  

And then I feel worse. Like I didn’t even get to be myself. Like I was just… performing.

Elizabeth, I really want you to hear something. You just described a really clear pattern, and you're seeing it honestly — that takes courage.

You open up. The response doesn't match what you hoped for. You feel the air leave the room. So you shrink, smile, and redirect. And then you're left feeling like you disappeared from your own life.

That's not "being too much." That's a protective response. Somewhere along the way, you learned that keeping the peace mattered more than taking up space. And when you try to step outside that — when you try to be real — the moment it feels unsafe, you go right back to what you know. Smile. Nod. Make it small.

But here's what strikes me. You said, *"I didn't even get to be myself."* You're not just describing one moment with your partner. You're describing something that feels bigger than that.

Can I ask — is this a pattern you recognize in other relationships too? Maybe even going back further than this one?

Yeah. I think it is.  

I remember in college, I’d tell people about my family stuff — not to complain, just to connect — and someone would say, “Wow, that’s intense,” or “You’re so dramatic,” and I’d just… stop. I’d laugh it off, change the subject. Like I’d said too much, like I’d made it weird.  

And then I’d start to think, maybe I *am* too much. Maybe I need to hold back. So I did. I started talking about the weather, or what I ate for lunch, or some random thing that didn’t matter.  

It felt safer. But over time, I started feeling… hollow. Like I wasn’t really there. Like I was just going through the motions.  

Now I’m older, and I still catch myself doing it. With my partner, with neighbors, even with coworkers. I’ll start to say something real, and then I’ll pause. I’ll think, *Wait — is this too much?* And then I’ll pull back.  

It’s like I’m always editing myself. And the more I do it, the harder it feels to say anything at all.

Elizabeth, what you're describing — the constant editing, the holding back, the shrinking — that's not a personality trait. That's a survival strategy. One you've been using for a long time.

And you're naming the cost really clearly. The hollowness. The going through the motions. The feeling of not being *there* in your own life. That's a profound thing to recognize.

I keep coming back to something you said — you started by talking about your *family stuff* in college. Not to complain, you said. Just to connect. And you got told you were dramatic. So you learned: real = too much. Safe = small.

But here's what I'm wondering. Before college — before anyone told you that — when you were younger, in your family growing up... what happened when you expressed something real? When you were upset, or excited, or needed something?

Because I'm guessing this didn't start in college. I'm guessing you already knew the steps to that dance by then.

You know… I don’t remember ever being told not to talk. Not really. My parents weren’t cold, but they weren’t the kind to sit around and say, “How are you *really*?”  

I used to tell my brother things — like when I was scared of the dark, or when a teacher was mean to me. He’d listen. He’d say, “That’s rough,” or “Yeah, that sucks.” And that was enough.  

But I also remember once, I came home crying over a fight with a friend, and my mom said, “It’s just a kid. Don’t make a big deal out of it.” And I just… stopped. Not because I didn’t want to talk, but because I realized — if I said it too loud, too long, it wasn’t welcome.  

So I started saving the big stuff. For him. For my brother.  

And now… I think I still do that. I save the real stuff. I wait for someone who feels safe. But I’m not always sure who that is.  

And when I finally say it — and it lands wrong — I don’t just feel dismissed. I feel like I’ve broken something. Like I messed up the connection.  

So I go quiet. I don’t want to risk it again.

Elizabeth, do you hear what you just did? You traced this all the way back. You found the moment.

*"Don't make a big deal out of it."*

That wasn't a cruel thing to say. Your mom probably didn't mean to shut you down. But you were a kid, and you were hurting, and you heard: *my feelings are an inconvenience.* So you made a decision — a really smart one, actually, for a kid — you found someone who would receive you. Your brother. And you saved the real stuff for him.

But here's the thing. You're 41 now. And you're still *saving* the real stuff. Still waiting for the safe person. Still holding your breath to see if it lands right.

And when it doesn't — when your partner says "it's not a big deal" — it doesn't just sting. It echoes. It echoes all the way back to that kitchen, that kid crying, that mom who didn't mean harm but couldn't meet you there.

You said when it lands wrong, you feel like you've *broken* something. But Elizabeth — what if the thing that's breaking isn't the connection? What if it's the *performance*? What if every time you shrink, something breaks inside *you*?

I'm curious about your brother. Are you still close? Is he still that safe person?

We talk every few weeks. Not every week, not like we used to. He’s got his own life — kids, work, a house on the other side of the county.  

I don’t tell him everything. Not like I used to.  

I’ll say things like, “I’ve been kind of tired lately,” or “Work’s been busy.” But I don’t say, *I feel like I’m losing myself*, or *I keep over-explaining just to be heard*.  

I don’t want to burden him. I don’t want him to think I’m too much.  

And I don’t know if he’d even know what to do with it. He’s not the kind to dive deep. He’s practical. He’d say, “Just take a break,” or “Maybe switch jobs.” And I’d be grateful, but I’d still feel… like I wasn’t really seen.  

Like I had to make it small enough to fit into his world.  

So I guess I’m not really sure if he’s still the safe person. Or if I just *need* him to be.  

Because if he’s not… then who is?

Elizabeth, I don't want to rush past that question. *"Then who is?"* That's the heart of what you're carrying.

And here's what strikes me. Even with your brother — the original safe person — you're still shrinking. Still editing. Still making it small enough to fit. The pattern didn't just follow you into your relationship. It followed you into the one place you thought was different.

So maybe the question isn't only *who* is the safe person. Maybe it's also: what would it feel like to say the real thing and *stay* — even when it doesn't land perfectly? Even when the other person doesn't know what to do with it?

Because here's what I'm noticing right now, Elizabeth. You just told me you feel like you're losing yourself. That you over-explain just to be heard. That you're not sure who's safe anymore.

You're not editing right now. You're not making it small. You're here. Being real.

So I want to ask — what feels different about this conversation? What's making it possible to say these things out loud right now?

I don’t know. I just… feel like I can. Not because I’m not scared. I am. I’m terrified, actually. But I also feel like… you’re not going to say “it’s not a big deal.”  

And that matters.  

I don’t know if I’ve ever said this out loud to someone who didn’t try to fix it or move on. You didn’t ask me to “just relax” or “stop overthinking.” You didn’t tell me to “let it go.” You just… listened. And asked questions that made me keep going.  

It feels like you’re not trying to change me. You’re just trying to see me.  

And that’s… rare.  

I think I’ve been so used to people saying “it’s not a big deal” or “just move on” that I forgot what it feels like to be seen without being fixed.  

So I guess… I’m not scared here. Not yet. Not like I usually am.  

I’m just… tired of being small.

Elizabeth. I want to sit with what you just said for a moment.

*"I'm tired of being small."*

That's not a small thing to say. That's someone who's been shrinking for decades — not because she wanted to, but because she thought she had to — finally naming the cost.

And you just named something really important. You said the difference wasn't that I have some special skill. The difference was that I didn't try to fix you, change you, or move you along. I just stayed.

That tells me something. You don't need people to say the perfect thing. You need people to *stay* in the room with you when you're real. That's it. That's the whole thing.

And you're right — I'm not going to tell you it's not a big deal. Because what you're describing *is* a big deal. It's the difference between existing and living.

So I want to ask you something. And I don't want you to overthink it.

When you imagine being less small — not loud, not dramatic, not a different person — just *less small*... what's one moment where that might look different? Maybe even this week. Something small, but real.

I don’t know. I keep thinking about my partner.  

He’s not bad. He’s kind. He just… doesn’t know how to sit with things. When I say something that feels heavy, he either changes the subject or gives me a solution.  

But I don’t want a solution. I just want him to say, “That sounds hard.”  

So maybe… maybe this week I’ll say it anyway. Just once.  

Not to fix anything. Not to make him do anything.  

Just to say, “I’ve been feeling really off lately. Not because something’s wrong, but because I feel like I’m not showing up the way I want to.”  

And then I’ll stop. I won’t explain. I won’t say why. I’ll just… leave it there.  

I don’t know if he’ll say anything. I don’t know if he’ll get it.  

But I want to try.  

Even if he doesn’t. Even if he says, “It’s not a big deal.”  

I want to say it anyway.  

Because I’m tired of being small.

Elizabeth, I want you to notice something about what you just said.

You didn't say, *"I'll explain why I feel this way."* You didn't say, *"I'll help him understand."* You said, *"I'll say it. And then I'll stop."*

That's not the old pattern. The old pattern was: say something real, then over-explain to make it acceptable, then when it doesn't land, shrink and smile.

You're doing something different. You're saying the true thing and letting it *be* true — whether he gets it or not.

And that last part — *"Even if he says it's not a big deal. I want to say it anyway."* That's new, Elizabeth. That's you choosing to take up your own space regardless of what happens next.

I think you already know this won't be easy. The hardest part won't be saying the words. It'll be the silence after. The moment where you want to fill the space, laugh it off, say *never mind.* That's the moment to watch for.

So here's my one thought. If he doesn't get it right — if he changes the subject or says it's not a big deal — what would you tell yourself in that moment? Because that's the moment that's always beaten you before. Not the saying it. The *after*.

I don’t know. I keep thinking I’ll say it, and then I’ll just… freeze. Like I’ll hear myself and think, *I went too far.*  

But what if I don’t? What if I just say it, and then I breathe? And then I say, “It’s okay. I said it.”  

I don’t need him to fix it. I don’t need him to agree.  

I just need to know I said it. That I didn’t shrink. That I didn’t make it small to fit in.  

So if he says it’s not a big deal… I could just say, “I know. But it felt big to me. And that’s enough.”  

Not to argue. Not to explain. Just… to stand there.  

And if I can do that — even once — I think I’ll remember it. And next time, I might not need to say it twice.

Elizabeth. I don't have much to add to what you just said. You just did the thing.

You found the words. Your words. Not over-explained. Not made small. Not wrapped in apologies or caveats.

*"I know. But it felt big to me. And that's enough."*

That's not a script. That's not something I gave you. That came from you. And it's exactly right — not because it'll make him understand, but because it's *true*.

You've spent this whole conversation doing what you said you wanted to do. You weren't small. You didn't edit yourself down. You said real things — hard things — and you stayed.

And I want you to hold onto one thing. If this week goes the way you hope, great. If it doesn't — if you freeze, if you shrink, if you laugh it off — that doesn't undo what happened here today. You already know what it feels like to say the real thing and stay in the room. That's in you now.

So here's my question as we wrap up. What would help you remember this conversation — this feeling — when you're standing in that moment with your partner, and the old pull to shrink shows up?

I don’t know if I’ll remember it. Not like I’m writing it down. But maybe… I could just text myself.  

Like, “You said it. You stayed. You didn’t shrink.”  

Or maybe I’ll keep a little note in my phone. Just one sentence.  

“I’m not too much. I just need to be seen.”  

Not for him. Not for anyone.  

For me.  

Because if I can remember that — even for a second — then maybe I can say it. Even if I’m scared. Even if I don’t know what comes next.  

I just need to know I can say it.  

And that’s enough.

Elizabeth. That's your sentence. You found it yourself.

*"I'm not too much. I just need to be seen."*

Write it down. Today. Don't wait. Put it in your phone, on a sticky note, wherever you'll see it. Because you're right — you won't remember this conversation word for word. But you'll remember that sentence. It's yours.

And I want you to know something. You came in today talking about heavy quiet. You're leaving having named something that's been running your life for thirty years. You traced it from your mom's kitchen, to college, to your partner, to right here. And then you practiced — right here, with me — what it looks like to say the real thing and stay.

That's not a small thing. That's the whole thing.

I'll be here, Elizabeth. Whenever you need to come back. Whether it goes well this week or it doesn't. Whether you said it and stayed, or you froze and shrank. Either way, come back and tell me what happened.

Because either way, you'll have shown up. And that's enough.

I’ll write it down. Right now.  

I’m opening my notes app. Typing it slow.  

“I’m not too much. I just need to be seen.”  

I’m reading it twice.  

And I’m not deleting it.  

I don’t know if I’ll remember it in the moment. But I’ll have it.  

And if I do — if I can say it — I’ll know I didn’t disappear.  

Even if just for a second.  

Thank you.
